questions.question_type: 全曲流派识别
questions.question: Taken as a whole, what broad musical style does this song most closely resemble? Which two sonic features support that judgment?
questions.reference_answer: It is closest overall to smooth jazz or mellow vocal jazz, with subtle bossa nova and blues inflections. Supporting features include the frequent use of extended chords such as maj7, 9, and 13, and the relaxed texture created by acoustic guitar, piano, bass, gentle percussion, flute, and muted trumpet. “Jazz pop” is also acceptable, but the piece should not be characterized definitively as pure Latin jazz or bossa nova.

questions.reference_answer: The lead vocal is male. The lowest notated pitch is E2, at the beginning of the bridge, and the highest is B4, in the first verse. questions.question_type: 整段和弦级数与扩展音分析
questions.question: Which chords occur from beginning to end in the first verse? What are their scale degrees, inversions, extensions, and principal connections in the home key?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is E major. Grouped by bar, the chord sequence is Em7–D♯m7–Dm7 | Emaj7 | Emaj7 | F♯m7–Amaj7/C♯ | F♯m7 | B9–B7/F♯ | B9 | Emaj7–Emaj7/B | Emaj7 | Emaj7–E13/B | Emaj7 | G♯7–G♯7/D♯ | G♯7 | F♯13 | F♯13 | B7–B9. In scale-degree and functional terms, Emaj7 is Imaj7 and Emaj7/B is Imaj7 in second inversion; F♯m7 is ii7; Amaj7/C♯ is IVmaj7 in first inversion; B7 and B9 are V7 and V9, and B7/F♯ is V4/3; G♯7 is V7/vi, and G♯7/D♯ is its second inversion, V4/3/vi; F♯13 is V13/V and proceeds at the end to B7–B9, creating a V/V→V dominant chain that remains on dominant function. The opening Em7–D♯m7–Dm7 consists of parallel descending chromatic minor-seventh chords: Em7 can be heard as borrowed i7 color from the parallel minor, while D♯m7 and Dm7 primarily provide chromatic passing and voice-leading connections. E13/B places the fifth B in the bass and contains the minor seventh D and the 13th C♯, giving it dominant-seventh extension color, although it does not resolve directly to A here. The passage is fundamentally organized around tonic function and a ii–V framework, with a secondary-dominant chain added in the middle; it ends in a half cadence rather than returning to I.

questions.question_type: 重属和弦与属功能链
questions.question: A continuous dominant-function chain occurs at the end of the second pre-chorus. Name its three chords, give their scale degrees in the song's home key, and identify the target of each step.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is F minor. G7/B is a first-inversion G dominant-seventh chord, labeled V6/5/V in F minor, and initially treats C7 as its temporary target. The full connection is therefore G7/B(V6/5/V)→C7(V7)→Fm(i), a V/V→V→i dominant chain that creates an authentic resolution rather than a modulation.

questions.question_type: 跨副歌主题与节奏变体比较
questions.question: Compare the same melodic theme at the openings of the first and second choruses. Which pitches and rhythms remain unchanged, and how do the entrance and the third bar change?
questions.reference_answer: Both retain the core figure B♭2 eighth–C3 eighth–D3 eighth–G3 eighth tied forward, followed in the next bar by G3 eighth–B♭3 quarter–C4 quarter–G3 quarter–G3 eighth. The first chorus leaves mostly empty space before this theme, whereas the second chorus first introduces an E♭3 quarter note and a one-beat rest. The third bar also changes: in the first chorus it is built mainly from an F3 quarter, a tied F3 quarter, another F3 quarter, and a rest; in the second it becomes an eighth rest, F3 dotted eighth, eighth rest, F3 dotted eighth, then extends to a G3 half note. Thus the core theme is repeated almost literally, but the second statement varies it through a new lead-in note, a fragmented F3 rhythm, and a longer G3 ending.

questions.question: In the first phrase of the bridge, count in four and identify where the vocal opening and the next principal notes enter. Why do these placements create a syncopated feel?

The first bar is z3 C3 B,2 z C3 z C z B,: after three sixteenth-note rests, C4 enters on the final sixteenth of beat 1 (1-a). questions.question_type: 主歌全部离调和弦分析
questions.question: Which clear non-diatonic chords occur in the second verse? What are their scale-degree origins, target chords, and actual functions in E♭ major?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is E♭ major. There are two clear types of non-diatonic chord. First is C7, or V7/ii, built from C–E–G–B♭; its target is Fm9(ii9), creating the brief tonicization C7(V7/ii)→Fm9(ii9). Second is B♭m6, which may be labeled borrowed v(add6). Its B♭–D♭–F minor-triad framework comes from the parallel key E♭ minor, while the added G remains diatonic to E♭ major. Rather than establishing a new key, it introduces darker color through D♭ and then returns to A♭maj7(IVmaj7). The remaining principal chords—E♭maj7(Imaj7), Fm7/Fm9(ii7/ii9), Gm7(iii7), and A♭maj7/A♭maj9(IVmaj7/IVmaj9)—all belong to the natural harmony of E♭ major.

questions.question: What is the complete chord progression of the second chorus? What are the scale degrees, inversions, and extensions of these chords, and in what harmonic state does the ending remain?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is B♭ major. In order, the progression is G7(♭9)–G | Cm7 | F–F/C | B♭maj7–B♭maj7/F | Gm7–Gm7/D | Cm7 | F | B♭maj7 | B♭maj7 sustained | E♭ | F7 | Dm7 | G7 | Cm7 | F(add11). In scale-degree and functional terms, G7(♭9) and G are V7(♭9)/ii and V/ii, initially tonicizing Cm7(ii7); F and F7 are V and V7, with F/C as the dominant in second inversion; B♭maj7 is Imaj7, and B♭maj7/F is the tonic chord in second inversion with F retained in the bass; Gm7 is vi7 and Gm7/D is vi7 in second inversion; E♭ is IV; Dm7 is iii7; and the later G7(V7/ii) again leads to Cm7(ii7). The passage ends on F(add11), or V(add11). Its added 11th B♭ has not yet resolved to the B♭ tonic, so the ending remains suspended on dominant function and can be heard as an open half cadence.

questions.question_type: 多次副歌终止策略比较
questions.question: How do the three chorus endings differ in their treatment of dominant tension? What are the key chords, scale degrees, and outcomes of each?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is E major. The first chorus ends on B7sus4→B7, or Vsus4→V7, without returning to E inside the chorus, so it has an open dominant-function close. The second chorus likewise begins its ending with B7sus4→B7, but changes within the same bar to A♯m7♭5. By root scale degree in E major, this can be labeled ♯ivø7; by spelling it also has viiø7/V color. The following section, however, begins not on the target B or the tonic E but on Amaj9(IVmaj9). A♯m7♭5 shares C♯, E, and G♯ with Amaj9, while only the bass moves down by semitone from A♯ to A, so its actual function is a chromatic neighbor chord that redirects dominant tension to IVmaj9. The potential label viiø7/V must not be used to claim that it has resolved to B. The third chorus clearly moves from B9(V9) to Emaj7(Imaj7), an authentic resolution from a ninth dominant to the tonic major-seventh chord. The three treatments are therefore dominant suspension, redirection or delay, and final resolution, with the last chorus providing the strongest arrival.

questions.reference_answer: The home key is E major. The bridge proceeds Amaj9(IVmaj9)→G♯m7(iii7)→Amaj9(IVmaj9)→G♯m7(iii7)→Amaj7(IVmaj7)→G♯m7(iii7)→C♯m7(vi7)→F♯m7(ii7)→B(V). The first four bars alternate IVmaj9 and iii7. The ninth B in Amaj9 and the major- and minor-seventh colors keep the harmony gentle and suspended. The second half moves through IVmaj7→iii7→vi7→ii7→V into a functional chain, with vi7→ii7→V in particular driving the harmony clearly toward the dominant. The bridge stops on B(V) without resolving to E(I) inside the section, preserving tension for the next chorus.

questions.question_type: 三次副歌主题变体比较
questions.question: Are the three choruses literal repetitions of the same core vocal passage, or do they retain its framework while changing it progressively? What specifically remains the same and changes in their opening two bars?
questions.reference_answer: They preserve the same melodic framework but are not mechanical copies. In E♭ major, the first two fully sung bars of the first chorus, bars 30–31, are B♭3 quarter–F4 quarter–F4 eighth–E♭4 quarter–B♭3 eighth tied forward, followed by B♭3 eighth, B♭3 eighth, F4 eighth, F4 eighth, E♭4 quarter, C4 quarter. The second chorus first adds an introductory bar 53 with G4–A♭4–G4–B♭3. Its core bar 54 matches the first chorus, and the first four eighth notes of bar 55 remain B♭3–B♭3–F4–F4, but the latter half changes to G4 quarter–C4 quarter in place of E♭4–C4. The third chorus also begins with an introductory bar. Bar 80 is B♭3 quarter, F4 quarter, F4 quarter, dotted-eighth rest, B♭3 sixteenth tied into the next bar. Bar 81 continues that tie with a B♭3 quarter, then F4 eighth, sixteenth rest, F4 sixteenth tied into an F4 quarter, and finally C4 quarter. These two bars omit E♭4 and rewrite the rhythm with longer values, short rests, and ties across the barline. The common anchor pitches in all three are B♭, F, and C; E♭ remains only in the first two, the second has a local pitch substitution, and the third omits E♭ while heightening syncopation and delay.

questions.reference_answer: The home key is E♭ major. A♭maj7 is IVmaj7, followed by A♭m6, borrowed from the parallel key E♭ minor as iv(add6). The latter chord contains A♭–C♭–E♭–F: its root remains A♭, F is the added sixth, and C♭ is the crucial chromatic pitch. IVmaj7→iv(add6) lowers C natural to C♭, creating the characteristic shadow of a minor subdominant. The harmony then moves to Gm7(iii7) and through C7(V7/ii) toward Fm7(ii7). This is mode mixture and voice leading, not modulation. The “6” here denotes an added sixth and must not be mistaken for figured bass indicating first inversion.

questions.question_type: 整段主歌和声与转位分析
questions.question: How does the first verse move among tonic, subdominant, and dominant functions from beginning to end? Give the exact chord, scale degree, inversion, and extension in every bar.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is E♭ major. Bars 5–19 are: 5 Fm9(ii9); 6 E♭maj7→E♭maj7/B♭(Imaj7→Imaj7 with the fifth in the bass, or second inversion); 7 E♭maj7(Imaj7); 8 Fm7→Fm7/C(ii7→ii4/3); 9 Fm7→Fm7/C(ii7→ii4/3); 10 B♭7→B♭7/F(V7→V4/3); 11 B♭7(V7); 12 E♭maj7→E♭maj7/B♭(Imaj7→Imaj7 in second inversion); 13 the same E♭maj7→E♭maj7/B♭; 14 E♭maj7→E♭maj7/B♭; 15 E♭maj7(Imaj7); 16 Fm7→Fm7/C(ii7→ii4/3); 17 Fm7→Fm/C(ii7→ii6/4, with the seventh omitted in the latter half); 18 B♭7→B♭7/F(V7→V4/3); 19 B♭7(V7). Thus the broad framework cycles among Imaj7, ii7/ii9, and V7. Bass inversions on B♭, C, and F smooth the bass line; the opening Fm9 is the only explicit ninth extension, and the verse contains no notated suspended chord. It ends on V7, postponing resolution until the next formal section.

questions.question_type: 三次副歌的复现与发展比较
questions.question: Compare the three choruses in sequence. How do their harmonic openings, orchestral layers, and degree of closure differ, and what structural role does each chorus play?
questions.reference_answer: The first chorus begins from the low-register center of Gm. Acoustic guitar, bass, drums, and percussion present the material directly, and the ending remains suspended on D. The second chorus enters in the B♭ region and adds keyboard, organ, and a more continuous bass line, resolving clearly to Gm for the first time at its end. The third chorus again begins in the brighter B♭ region, layering two guitars, keyboard, and synthesizer pad while the voice rises into a higher register. Its main vocal portion closes fully with D7→Gm and is followed by a longer instrumental extension. The three choruses therefore serve, in order, as presentation, expansion, and climax with prolongation rather than literal repetition.

questions.question_type: 副歌半音和声与真实去向分析
questions.question: Give the chordal framework and scale degrees of the main vocal portion of the third chorus. Distinguish the chords that produce genuine dominant resolutions from the chord used only for chromatic color.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is G minor. The main framework is B♭–B7–G/B–Cm–F–B♭–Dm/A–Gm–Cm–D7–Gm, corresponding to III–♯III7–V6/iv–iv–VII–III–v6/4–i–iv–V7–i. G/B, as V6/iv, genuinely resolves to Cm, and D7, containing F♯, genuinely resolves as V7 to Gm. B7 is a chromatic dominant-seventh color chord rooted on the raised third degree and can be labeled ♯III7. Its own dominant tendency would normally point to Em, but it actually moves to G/B while retaining B in the bass, so it serves as a common-bass color connection rather than a completed secondary-dominant resolution. Dm/A is the natural-minor v in second inversion and actually resolves to Gm.

questions.question_type: 三次副歌长度与内部留白比较
questions.question: The three choruses use similar material, but which one functions as a shortened transition, and which inserts an instrumental gap in the middle and achieves the fullest closure? Describe the structural differences you hear.
questions.reference_answer: The first chorus gives a complete nine-bar statement, with the lead vocal unfolding continuously and then leaving three beats of rest after the final D♯4 quarter note. The second chorus is only seven bars long. It uses the familiar opening material but moves into the bridge early at the point where another turnaround is expected, making it the shortened transition. questions.question: Give the bridge's chord framework and scale degrees. How do its key chromatic chords connect the surrounding harmony, and where do they actually lead?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is B♭ major. questions.question_type: 全曲拍组与律动特征识别
questions.question: How many beats make up the recurring metric group across the song? How does that grouping affect the melody's rocking motion?
questions.reference_answer: The song is in 3/4, with three beats per bar. Each cycle generally places stability on the first beat while the second and third beats continue the motion, and sustained notes often fill all three beats. The melody therefore has a continuous three-beat sway rather than a four-beat pop groove. It may be heard as a modern three-beat ballad, but need not be equated mechanically with a traditional waltz.

questions.question: Compare the phrase length, use of repetition, and instrumental focus of the three choruses. What structural role does each one play?
questions.reference_answer: The first chorus is the most compact, completing one statement of the core melody in roughly eight bars, supported by synthesizer pad, bass, drums, and electric guitar. The second is clearly longer: it develops the same core phrase again, adds acoustic guitar, flute, organ, and electric piano, and finishes with an additional extended low-register close. After the bridge, the third chorus is the longest. It begins with a short transitional entrance, restates the core melody in several phrases, and finally settles through an extended B♭–F descent. Its instrumentation is actually more focused on drums, bass, electric piano, and electric guitar, allowing the lead vocal's high register to become the center of attention. The three roles are presentation, expansion, and final return.

questions.question: On which metrical position does the first bar of the first chorus begin singing? How do the consecutive short notes push the final pitch across the barline?

questions.question: The second chorus largely retains the melody of the first, but two harmonic recolorings are crucial. First identify the home key, then locate both substitutions, state their Roman numerals or functions and actual successors, and explain why the melody remains coherent over them.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is F major. In the first substitution, C♯dim replaces the corresponding Em7 in the first chorus. C♯dim has leading-tone function toward Dm and can be labeled vii°/vi; it actually moves first to A7, V7/vi, and then to Dm7, vi7, intensifying the motion toward the relative minor. In the second substitution, the first chorus's B♭m, borrowed iv, becomes a B♭ major triad, IV, followed by C, V, and F, I, producing a brighter color. At these points, both melodies still use common tones and stepwise motion around G, F, E and C, B♭ as their framework, so the chord changes do not obscure the melody's identity.

questions.reference_answer: The home key is B♭ minor. The progression is B♭m (i)–E♭m (iv)–A♭ (VII)–D♭maj7/D♭ (IIImaj7/III)–G♭6 [VI(add6)]–Fm (v)–A♭/A♭6 [VII/VII(add6)]–B♭m7 (i7)–E♭m7–E♭m6 [iv7–iv(add6)]–G♭9–Fsus4–F (Vsus4–V). Each chord labeled “6” is an added-sixth chord, not a first-inversion Roman numeral. G♭9 is a color chord built on scale degree VI with an added minor seventh and ninth; it actually moves to Fsus4 rather than establishing G♭ as a key. The real connections include G♭6→Fm, A♭6→B♭m7, and E♭m6→G♭9→Fsus4→F. The final F major triad, V, resolves to B♭m, i, at the start of the next section, creating a clear dominant-to-tonic resolution.

questions.question_type: 全局主中心与功能和声证据
questions.question: The opening harmony briefly leaves the tonic center ambiguous. After hearing the entire track, which key should be heard as its ultimate home? Use recurring cadential progressions, one secondary-dominant progression, and the final arrival to explain why the opening color chords do not establish another key.
questions.reference_answer: The track ultimately settles in D major. The verses and choruses repeatedly use Em7–A (or A7)–D, ii7–V (or V7)–I, its most stable return progression. F♯m7–B7–Em7 is iii7–V7/ii–ii7: B7 actually resolves to Em7 rather than establishing B major. The bridge also contains Em7–E7–A7, in which E7 is V7/V and actually moves to A7, V7, before the final chorus and ending continue toward D. The closing instrumental loop lands on the D tonic through Em7–A–D, ii7–V–I. Opening colors such as F♯maj7, A/F♯, and Gm7 do not sustain any new dominant–tonic confirmation, nor does the music maintain a new tonic afterward. They therefore create only temporary ambiguity and do not displace D major as the tonal center.

questions.question: How does the final chorus expand the earlier, shorter chorus material into the track's concluding climax? Address the melodic register, rhythmic density, and the extension after the vocal ends.
questions.reference_answer: The vocal part begins around G3 and F♯3, then gradually rises through B3, C♯4, and D4, reaching its high point at D4. After the vocal ends, an entire instrumental cycle of Em7–A–F♯m7–B7–Em7–A–D remains. The climax is therefore created both by the rising register and broadened note values and by the extended instrumental ending.

questions.question_type: 三次副歌旋律与节奏发展
questions.question: The three choruses are not simple successive copies. Compare their melodic high points, distribution of rests, and added closing phrases, then summarize how the theme develops across its three appearances.
questions.reference_answer: The first chorus states the theme for eight measures in the middle and lower registers, then adds a four-measure high closing phrase in which the melody leaps to D5 and continues to E5, the track's most conspicuous high point. The second chorus retains the first eight measures of the theme but omits this high extension and closes with a shorter phrase on D. The third chorus still preserves the same thematic contour, but breaks many sustained notes into short notes and rests, with more space at the entrance and within phrases, and adds a shorter closing phrase. It consequently sounds more fragmented rather than simply repeating the first chorus's high-register climax.

questions.question_type: 四句高音尾句的骨干听写
questions.question: The end of the first chorus contains four high-register extension phrases. Give their principal pitches and rhythms, identify the highest pitch and the final sustained pitch, and treat notes tied across barlines as equivalent longer values where appropriate. questions.reference_answer: The four phrases can be summarized as four measures of 4/4: (1) D4 quarter note, D5 eighth note, C♯5 quarter note, D5 quarter note, and B4 eighth note tied into the next phrase; (2) the tied B4 continues for another eighth note, producing the effect of a quarter note across the barline, followed by A4 as two tied eighth notes, G4 as two tied eighth notes, F♯4 eighth note, and D4 quarter note; (3) D4 quarter note, D5 eighth note, C♯5 as two tied eighth notes, D5 quarter note, and E5 eighth note; (4) B4–B4–A4–A4–F♯4–F♯4 as eighth notes, followed by a final sustained F♯4 quarter note. The highest pitch is E5, and the final point of repose is F♯4. Combining the tied B4 and the adjacent A4, G4, and C♯5 pairs into equivalent quarter notes preserves the same rhythmic meaning.

questions.question_type: 主歌半音和弦及实际去向
questions.question: Why is the first verse's harmony more unsettled than an ordinary natural-minor progression? List its analytically significant chromatic chords, give each chord's function or source in the home key and its actual successor, and summarize how they ultimately return to the tonic center.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is E minor. The opening Am7–D7–Gmaj9 is iv7–V7/III–IIImaj9, briefly establishing the relative major, G. F♯m7♭5, iiø7, could lead to B7 but instead slips first to Fmaj7/C. Fmaj7/C is a second-inversion ♭IImaj7 with C, its fifth, in the bass; it can be heard as Neapolitan-like chromatic passing color. It actually moves to B7, V7, which resolves to Em7, i7. Later, F♯7 and C7 create a coloristic chromatic juxtaposition: F♯7 may be heard as V7/V but actually moves first to C7; C7 may be labeled VI7 with a lowered seventh in E minor, or ♭VI7 by reference to the parallel major, and actually returns to F♯7. Only the second C7 moves to B7, V7. The following Bmaj7 may be labeled a Vmaj7 color on the dominant scale degree; it returns to B7 without becoming the tonic of B major. Dominant function is thus kept in suspension to prepare the next chorus's return to Em, i.

questions.question: How do the register and melodic direction at the openings of the three choruses differ? Explain how the final entrance returns to the original thematic register afterward.

It thus strengthens the sense of return without introducing a different theme.

questions.question: How does the bridge melody gradually build tension from a relatively narrow middle register? Summarize the pitch focus in the first half, the manner of ascent later on, and the direction of the final phrase.
questions.reference_answer: The first half repeatedly centers on C4, D4, and E♭4 within a narrow range. In the middle, F4 is added to repeated-note and stepwise figures, gradually raising the registral focus. questions.question_type: 末次副歌完整功能进行
questions.question: Provide a complete harmonic analysis of the final chorus: identify the home key, specific chords, and Roman numerals; state the opening dominant chord's actual successor; and explain how the ending reconverges on tonic function.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is C minor. The opening G7 is V7, but it actually moves first to Fm, iv, prolonging dominant tension rather than immediately proceeding V7–i. Bb, VII, then moves to Eb, III, before Bb/D, VII6, leads to Cm, i. The middle proceeds through Fm (iv)–Bb (VII)–Cm (i), followed by Fm7 (iv7)–Bb (VII)–Eb (III)–Ab (VI)–Fm (iv). The G major triad at the end is V and leaves its tension to resolve to Cm, i, in the next section. The framework can therefore be summarized as V7–iv–VII–III–VII6–i, followed by motion around iv, VII, III, and VI, and finally iv–V–i into the ending section.

questions.reference_answer: All three choruses can be heard as returns of the same core theme. Their shared marker is the ascending entrance A3–B♭3–C4; C4 is then prolonged, and the next phrase passes near A3 before moving to F4–E4. In the middle of the first chorus, F3 replaces an A3 found in the second and third, and the entrance durations differ slightly, but these local variations do not alter the theme's identity.

questions.reference_answer: The first verse retains only acoustic guitar and bass and therefore has the thinnest texture. The first chorus adds drums, organ, flute, and synthesizer, creating a full-bandwidth sound for the first time. The second chorus brings in electric guitar, piano, and synth pad, continuing the dynamic growth while remaining one regular cycle in length. The final chorus restates the theme with drums, bass, electric guitar, keyboard, and synth layers, then adds a longer instrumental loop after the core vocal material. It is therefore broader in timbre and provides the final temporal expansion.

questions.question: A raised melodic pitch briefly changes the tonal color in the second chorus. What is the pitch, how does it continue across the chord boundary, and how does the inverted bass in the accompaniment subsequently resolve?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is F major. The raised melodic pitch is C♯4. It appears at the end of a B♭ chord and is tied across the barline into the beginning of A7/C♯. Rather than moving directly to D4, this vocal pitch then proceeds through E4–G4–A4. Harmonically, A7/C♯ is V6/5/vi, the first inversion of A7. Its bass C♯ continues under A7 and then rises to D, the root of the following Dm chord. questions.question_type: 桥段局部和声重心与解决链
questions.question: The bridge contains two local harmonic centers. First identify the track's home key, then give the complete principal progression, Roman numerals, and actual destinations of each dominant-function chord, and determine whether this amounts to a global modulation.
questions.reference_answer: The home key remains F major. The principal progression begins with A7 (V7/vi)–Dm (vi), followed by Dm–Cm7–F–B♭, or vi–v7/IV–I/IV–IV; within this, Cm7–F is ii7/IV–V/IV pointing to B♭. The latter half is Gm7–A7–Dm–Dm7/C–Gm7, or ii7–V7/vi–vi–vi4/2–ii7. Both A7 chords actually resolve to Dm, briefly emphasizing D minor, while Cm7–F actually resolves to B♭, briefly emphasizing IV. The key signature and ultimate tonal center do not change, and the following section still enters through F-major functions such as C and F. These are therefore local tonicizations, not a full modulation.

questions.question_type: 全局主中心与跨段和声证据
questions.question: After hearing the full track, what are its most stable tonic center and mode? Cite one actual progression each from the introduction, verse, and bridge or ending, and explain why the other frequently recurring minor chord does not replace the main tonal center.
questions.reference_answer: The tonal center is B♭ and the mode is B♭ major. The introduction unfolds as B♭–Gm–E♭–B♭, I–vi–IV–I, establishing B♭ as the destination of the opening loop. The first verse is built around B♭–F/A–Gm–E♭–F, I–V6–vi–IV–V; the dominant function of F or F7 repeatedly directs the music back to B♭. The bridge repeatedly uses F–B♭, V–I, and its latter half includes B♭–B♭maj7/A–Gm–E♭–F–B♭, I–I4/2–vi–IV–V–I, before the closing instrumental loop returns to B♭. questions.reference_answer: Three moments are especially clear. First, the phrase over F♯m7 begins after an eighth-note rest, with A3 entering on the second half of beat 1 rather than on the downbeat. Second, E4 in the following Em7 measure begins on the second half of beat 4 and is tied across the barline into beat 1 of the A7 measure. An earlier F♯3 at the end of an A7 phrase also ties across the barline to Dmaj7. questions.reference_answer: The home key is D major. The inserted chord is B♭m, which may be labeled the chromatic minor triad ♭vi. The first time it appears at the end of an A-chord phrase and moves immediately to Dmaj7, I; the second time it is similarly inserted after the A region and again moves to Dmaj7. B♭m receives no dominant–tonic support and does not sustain B♭ minor. Its voices can move chromatically from around A/C♯ to B♭/D♭ and back to D/F♯, so it functions more like a coloristic neighboring or passing chord before the tonic. questions.question_type: 末次副歌调性变化判断与证据
questions.question: Compare the tonality of the final chorus with the preceding sections. If the tonal center changes, identify the keys before and after, the pivot-point chords and Roman numerals, and use the material that persists afterward as proof. If it does not change, explain why the passage is only a local tonicization rather than a modulation.
questions.reference_answer: The first part is in D major, and the final chorus genuinely modulates up a semitone to E♭ major. Before the shift, the music prolongs A, V in D major, and creates lift with the semitone ascent A–A♯. In the new key, a B♭ major triad becomes V and immediately moves to E♭ major, I, confirming the new key with V–I. The music then consistently uses Cm7 (vi7), Fm7 (ii7), A♭m (borrowed iv), and B♭7sus4 (V7sus4), and the subsequent improvisation and ending continue to revolve around E♭, Cm, Fm, and A♭m. This is therefore a stable new tonic center, not a one-off chromatic chord rise.

The second half begins with D7, V7/IV, but instead of proceeding conventionally to G, it turns to G♯m7♭5. G♯m7♭5–C♯7–F♯m7 then forms iiø7/iii–V7/iii–iii7, tonicizing iii. questions.question_type: 器乐主奏听写与单元关系判断
questions.question: The instrumental section can be heard as two four-measure units. Reconstruct the main pitches and durations of the first unit, explain how ties across barlines connect the phrase, and determine whether the second unit is an exact repeat, a transposition, or a local variation. Where does the change occur?
questions.reference_answer: The first unit may be summarized as follows: (1) C♯4 eighth note, D♯4 tied for a total of three beats, then G♯3 eighth note at the end tied into the next measure; (2) the tied G♯3 produces the effect of a dotted quarter note, followed by D♯3 dotted quarter note, E3 eighth note, D♯3 eighth note, and tied A♯3 eighth note; (3) the tied A♯3 likewise produces a dotted-quarter effect, followed by D♯3 quarter note, then D♯4–E4–D♯4–F♯3 as four eighth notes, with F♯3 tied into the next phrase; (4) the tied F♯3 is followed by D♯3 quarter note, C♯4 eighth note, C♯4 quarter note, and a B3 eighth note tied onward. The four phrases use G♯m–C♯m–F♯–D♯m, i–iv–VII–v. The second unit is neither transposed nor repeated exactly. Its first measure prolongs the B3 tied in from the preceding measure and then closes with D♯3–E3–D♯3–G♯3 as four eighth notes; only its remaining three measures reproduce measures 2–4 of the first unit note for note and rhythm for rhythm. It is therefore a local variation that rewrites only the opening measure of the second unit.

questions.question_type: 非功能性属七色彩与真实去向
questions.question: One seventh chord in the second chorus sounds distinctly darker than its counterpart in the first. Identify it, give its Roman numeral in the home key and its actual successor, and determine whether it completes a conventional dominant resolution.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is A♭ major. The darker chord is D♭7, or IV7. It adds the chromatic minor seventh C♭ to the original D♭ major triad. Its actual successor is Fm, vi, rather than G♭, the conventional target if D♭7 were acting as a dominant seventh. It therefore does not complete a standard dominant-seventh resolution and functions primarily as a coloristic harmonic alteration.

questions.question_type: 桥段和声展开与跨段回归
questions.question: How does the bridge use the track's core chords to create a longer development? Give its principal Roman-numeral path and explain how the chord prolonged at the end reconnects to the next section.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is A♭ major. The bridge begins A♭–D♭–Fm–E♭, I–IV–vi–V, and then passes again through I–IV–vi. Once the main melody enters, it follows E♭–D♭–E♭–Fm–A♭–D♭–E♭–D♭–D♭, or V–IV–V–vi–I–IV–V–IV–IV. The ending prolongs D♭, IV, and the next section actually returns to A♭, I. The bridge therefore does not close immediately with V–I; it suspends the motion on the subdominant, and the following section's tonic completes the return.

questions.question_type: 主歌完整和声、转位与延迟副属分析
questions.question: Listen to the second verse and give a complete account of its harmonic path: identify the home key, a compressed chord framework and Roman numerals, two analytically significant types of bass inversion, and why the strongest secondary dominant at the end does not resolve immediately but reaches its target across the section boundary.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is B major. Compressed by distinct harmonic events, the second verse is E/B–B–D♯m–E–B–F♯/A♯–G♯m–D♯m–C♯m7–F♯sus4–F♯–B–D♯m–E–B–F♯/A♯–G♯m–C♯7–Emaj7, corresponding to IV6/4–I–iii–IV–I–V6–vi–iii–ii7–Vsus4–V–I–iii–IV–I–V6–vi–V7/V–IVmaj7. The opening E/B is IV in second inversion, IV6/4, and actually returns to the B tonic. Both F♯/A♯ chords are first-inversion dominants, V6: their bass A♯ rises to B, but each actually leads to G♯m, vi, creating a deceptive resolution of the dominant. The closing C♯7 is II7 with the function V7/V; although it should lead to F♯, V, it first moves to Emaj7, IVmaj7. The next section only then enters through F♯sus4 and F♯, so the target dominant is delayed until after the section boundary.

Both have a short instrumental response after their openings, but the second adds one extra measure of instrumental response supported by Dm in the middle before returning to the familiar melodic contour. questions.question_type: 无根副属和弦延长分析
questions.question: Why do the two tense chords at the end of the second verse sound like parts of the same directional chain? Give their functions in the home key and their actual destination.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is F major. D7 appears first: it is VI7 with the function V7/ii, targeting Gm. Rather than reaching Gm immediately, it moves to Cdim7. Cdim7 consists of C–E♭–G♭–A and can be heard enharmonically as a rootless D7(♭9), continuing the tension of V7(♭9)/ii. The next section actually lands on Gm7, ii7. The complete effect is D7→Cdim7→Gm7: secondary-dominant function is prolonged by rootless diminished-seventh color before resolving to ii.

questions.question_type: 副歌半音和声框架分析
questions.question: Why is the harmony of the first chorus more dramatic than that of the verse? Give its principal chord framework, identify its two crucial chromatic chords, and state where each one actually goes.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is F major. The framework is F–B♭maj7–D♭+–Am7–D7–Dm7/F–Gm7–C6–C7, or I–IVmaj7–♭VI+–iii7–V7/ii–vi6/5–ii7–V(add6)–V7. D♭+, consisting of D♭–F–A, is a chromatic augmented triad on the lowered sixth scale degree and actually moves to Am7, iii7. The chords share A, while D♭ descends to C and F descends to E, creating two chromatic lines. D7 would normally target Gm but changes first to Dm7/F and only then reaches Gm7, delaying the secondary-dominant tension through a major-to-minor-third change on the same root. The final C6–C7 reinforces dominant function in preparation for the subsequent F tonic.

questions.question_type: 借用小下属与半音声部进行
questions.question: Which chord produces the first verse's clearest shift from bright to dark? What kind of borrowing is it, and how do its bass and inner voices lead toward the subsequent relative-minor region?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is F major. The darkening chord is B♭m6, whose pitch collection is B♭–D♭–F–G; it is the borrowed minor subdominant with added sixth, iv(add6). The actual progression is B♭m6→Am→Dm7, or iv(add6)→iii→vi7. In the core voices of the first two triads, B♭ descends to A, D♭ to C, and F to E, producing three chromatic descending lines, while the added G acts as a suspension or passing color. The harmony therefore moves first to Am rather than directly back to F, then enters the relative-minor region through Dm7.

questions.question_type: 疑似转调的听觉核验
questions.question: Does the short transition before the final chorus genuinely establish a new tonic? Base your judgment on the transition's chords and the final chorus's stable arrival points.
questions.reference_answer: The available score evidence does not support a genuine modulation. The home key is B♭ major. The short transition uses B♭, E♭maj7, Cm6, F, and Fsus4 before returning to B♭ and E♭maj7, corresponding to I, IVmaj7, ii(add6), V, Vsus4, I, and IVmaj7. Cm6 consists of C–E♭–G–A and remains a minor chord rooted on scale degree ii, not a slash chord with F in the bass. The final chorus continues to center on B♭–F–Gm–Dm–E♭–F, I–V–vi–iii–IV–V, and returns to B♭, I. The transition therefore provides predominant–dominant preparation and registral expansion within the original key rather than establishing another tonic.

questions.reference_answer: The home key is A major. The local chain is Bm7–F+–C♯+–A–C♯–F♯m, or ii7–♭VI+–III+–I–III–vi. F+ is spelled F–A–C♯ and actually moves to C♯+; C♯+ is spelled C♯–E♯–G𝄪 and is still enharmonically C♯–F–A. The two augmented triads are therefore differently named interpretations of the same symmetrical pitch collection, requiring almost no change in sounding pitch at their connection. C♯+ then moves to the A major tonic, I, retaining A and C♯ while E♯ descends to E; it does not resolve directly to F♯m. questions.reference_answer: The home key is C major. The harmonic framework is C-E7-Am-F-C-Dm-G-C-E-Am-G-Fm-C-G, corresponding to I-V7/vi-vi-IV-I-ii-V-I-V/vi-vi-V-iv-I-V. The final G is V and carries forward into the next section before resolving.

questions.question: Listen to the end of the first chorus. What are its final two chords, what are their scale degrees in the home key, and why is this close weaker than a traditional dominant–tonic cadence?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is C♯ minor, and the final two chords are B-C♯m, or VII-i. questions.question_type: 三次副歌的起句与收束比较
questions.question: Across the song, compare the opening entry, length, and final harmonic destination of the three choruses. Why does the last chorus sound the most complete?
questions.reference_answer: The first chorus lasts 8 measures. After a relatively long opening space, it enters with three eighth notes, B♭3–C4–E♭4; it ends by moving from A♭ to B♭ and stops on the dominant. The second chorus is shortened to 7 measures: it begins with a brief E♭4, pauses, and then returns to B♭3–C4–E♭4; its Cm-to-B♭ ending likewise retains an unresolved quality. The third chorus expands to 14 measures. Over a B♭ chord, it opens with F4, B♭4, and a string of G4s to create a wider-ranging introduction, then returns to the familiar melody and adds an extended tail before finally landing on the tonic E♭ chord. Its greater length, heightened opening tension, and tonic resolution make the third chorus the most conclusive.

Its brightness comes from frequent C and G chords: in Am-C-G-F, C is III and G is VII, while repeated C-G can evoke I-V in C major. questions.question_type: 完整副歌和声与低音线条分析
questions.question: Listen to the first chorus. Write out its complete harmonic framework and Roman numerals, then analyze one deceptive progression and the actual destination of the bass inversion near the end.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is G major. The harmonic framework is Am-D-G-D-Em-Bm-C-G-Gmaj7-Em-Bm-Am-D-Em-Bm-C-G-Gmaj7/F♯-Em-Am-D-G, corresponding to ii-V-I-V-vi-iii-IV-I-Imaj7-vi-iii-ii-V-vi-iii-IV-I-Imaj7(4/2)-vi-ii-V-I. Early in the section, D/V does not return to G/I but actually moves to Em/vi, forming a V-vi deceptive progression. Later, Gmaj7/F♯ is the third inversion of the tonic major-seventh chord, with its seventh F♯ in the bass; that bass moves down to the root E of Em, creating a smooth Imaj7(4/2)→vi bass connection. The final Am-D-G closes fully with ii-V-I.

questions.question_type: 全局主调与关系小调色彩识别
questions.question: Listen to the entire song. What is its most stable home key, and why do the recurring chords from the relative key not displace that primary center?
questions.reference_answer: The primary center is C major. Much of the song alternates between C and Am, with Am functioning as vi in C major. Most sections unfold from C, and the bridge adds F/IV and G/V, clarifying the I-IV-V framework of C major. Am supplies relative-minor color, but it remains primarily one side of an I-vi loop rather than establishing A minor through an independent dominant–tonic relation such as E7-Am.

questions.question_type: 三次副歌配器层次与收束方式比较
questions.question: While preserving the core theme, how do the accompaniment layers and sectional endings change across the three choruses? Compare the most prominent timbral combination in each, and identify which chorus most clearly serves as the song's climax and endpoint.
questions.reference_answer: The first chorus builds its rock foundation from acoustic guitar, bass, and drums, then layers organ, piano, and electric guitar on top, expanding the theme into a full-band texture for the first time; only a very short instrumental tail follows. The second retains acoustic guitar, drums, bass, and electric guitar, but a synthesizer chiefly replaces the sustained organ-and-piano colors. It ends after one compact pass through the theme, without a long instrumental tail. The third uses drums, bass, acoustic guitar, percussion, organ, and electric piano; the vocal theme itself is repeated and extended, and a long instrumental passage follows the vocal, continuing the accompaniment pattern over C and Am. By expanding the keyboard colors, percussion layer, and total duration at once, the final chorus functions as both the song's largest climax and its ultimate close.

questions.question_type: 完整桥段和声框架与阻碍进行分析
questions.question: Listen to the bridge. Write out its complete harmonic framework and Roman numerals. Explain where the newly introduced functional chords actually lead and how the latter half returns to the song's core loop.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is C major. After consecutive repetitions are combined, the bridge's harmonic framework is F-C-F-C-G-Am-C-Am-C-Am, corresponding to IV-I-IV-I-V-vi-I-vi-I-vi. The song's earlier core is largely the C-Am I-vi loop. The bridge first expands the subdominant area with F/IV, then creates the strongest dominant tension with G/V; rather than landing on C, however, G actually moves to Am/vi, forming a V-vi deceptive progression. The harmony then returns to the C-Am I-vi alternation, and the final Am/vi leads into C/I at the next chorus.

questions.question: From the opening through the final chorus, what key changes occur in the accompaniment's density and timbre? Identify the leading instruments in at least three stages and explain why the last section is the thickest.
questions.reference_answer: The opening combines piano, harp, strings, and violin in a transparent, chamber-like texture. questions.reference_answer: After each entrance, all three choruses retain the A3–C4–A3 core, pause for an eighth rest, repeat A3 several times, and descend to G3. Bass and drums form the rhythmic and low-frequency foundation, while electric guitar adds another electric layer. The opening is therefore not a solo acoustic-guitar passage, but a four-layer combination with acoustic guitar in front, bass and drums underneath, and electric guitar adding color.

questions.question: At the end of the third verse, a secondary dominant is first suspended and then released. Which scale degree is suspended, how does it resolve, and which chord in the next section does the released harmony actually target?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is E major. The progression is C#7sus4 to C# (understandable as a C#7 resolution with the seventh omitted): the suspended F# is a fourth above the root C# and resolves downward to E#, the chord's third, producing a 4–3 resolution. In E major, the C# chord is V/ii; it actually points to and lands on F#m7, ii7, in the next section.

The chorus ends on the dominant B, V, and the following outro begins on the tonic E, I, completing a V—I resolution across the section boundary.

questions.question_type: 终副歌完整和声路线分析
questions.question: Beginning with the vocal entry and continuing through the closing instrumental accompaniment, list the complete chord path and Roman numerals of the final chorus. Then explain how the first half returns to the tonic and why the second half sounds as though it reopens the loop.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is D minor. The complete chord sequence is A—Dm—Gm—C—F—Bb—Gm—A—A—Dm—Gm—C—F, corresponding to V—i—iv—VII—III—VI—iv—V—V—i—iv—VII—III. The prolonged A (V) at the opening immediately resolves to Dm (i). The latter part of the vocal again stops on A (V), which the accompaniment resolves to Dm (i), but it continues to Gm—C—F (iv—VII—III). The ending therefore does not seal the section on the tonic; instead, it opens the minor-key loop into the relative-major region. Every annotated chord is a root-position triad, with no suspended or seventh chords.

questions.question_type: 副歌与桥段配器发展
questions.question: Although the first chorus, second chorus, and bridge share a similarly warm foundation, their instrumentation changes color progressively. Compare the core instrumental combinations in the three sections and explain how their energy and texture change.
questions.reference_answer: The first chorus combines acoustic guitar, bass, electric guitar, and ukulele. Its many plucked timbres remain light because no full drum kit is present. The second chorus adds drums and piano around an acoustic-guitar and bass foundation, producing a firmer groove and fuller harmony. The bridge retains acoustic guitar, bass, and drums while adding percussion, harp, and ukulele; rather than simply growing heavier, it preserves forward momentum while adding shimmering, gentle colors.

questions.question_type: 桥段和弦进行与变化音分析
questions.question: Write out the bridge's complete chord progression and Roman numerals. Identify the lead vocal's highest chromatic note over the secondary dominant, explain where that dominant actually moves, and state how the music ultimately returns to the tonic.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is F major. The bridge chords are F—F—A7—A7—Bb—C—F, corresponding to I—I—V7/vi—V7/vi—IV—V—I. Over A7, the lead vocal reaches C#5, both the section's highest note and the major third of A7, clearly showing that the chord is not Am. Conventionally, A7 would move to Dm (vi), but here it actually proceeds to Bb (IV), after which C—F completes a V—I authentic resolution. The secondary-dominant tension is thus redirected toward the subdominant region before the music finally returns to the tonic F chord.

questions.question_type: 后半曲式重建与终副歌扩展
questions.question: After the second chorus, how does the song rebuild energy in three stages instead of immediately repeating its close? Why does the final chorus resemble an expanded concluding chapter more than the first two?
questions.reference_answer: After the second chorus, the song first enters a thickened instrumental passage driven by drums, synth bass, synth lead, strings, and electric guitar. The bridge then rebuilds tension with new melodic organization and denser synthesizer and percussion, before the third chorus finally arrives. The first two choruses last roughly 17 and 15 measures, respectively, whereas the final chorus expands to about 29 measures: its first 17 measures continue the chorus's vocal material, followed by a 12-measure instrumental harmonic tail. It therefore both restates the theme and brings the full song to a close.

questions.question_type: 桥段开头旋律的连线与留白组织
questions.question: Listen to the first four measures after the vocal enters in the bridge. How do ties across barlines and rests shape the phrasing? Identify the notes that actually cross the barline and the most prominent points of silence.
questions.reference_answer: In C♯ minor and 4/4, the structural outline of the first four vocal measures is G♯4-A4-A4-G♯4-F♯4 | F♯4-rest-F♯4-G♯4 | G♯4-G♯4-G♯4-F♯4-E4 | E4-long rest. F♯4, G♯4, and E4 each begin as an eighth note at the end of one measure and tie to an eighth note at the start of the next, totaling a quarter note each time. The first continued F♯4 is followed immediately by a half rest, while the third continued E4 is followed by fourteen sixteenth-note units, or three and a half beats, of rest. The phrases therefore do not restart at every barline: ties connect local units, and long gaps articulate the internal breathing points and phrase ending.

questions.reference_answer: The earlier first verse uses only bass and acoustic guitar, while drums, piano, electric guitar, or organ are gradually introduced in the chorus. questions.question_type: 全曲段落配器重心比较
questions.question: Across the entire song, compare the instrumental emphasis in the first verse–chorus cycle, the second verse–chorus cycle, and the outro. Which foundational instruments remain throughout, and how do the foreground colors rotate among the stages?
questions.reference_answer: Bass and drums continue through all five sections, forming the persistent low-frequency and rhythmic foundation. The first verse uses foreground electric guitar, strings, and synthesizer pad to create a sustained texture; the first chorus changes color with acoustic guitar, piano, and synthesizer. The second verse juxtaposes acoustic guitar, electric guitar, and synthesizer, whereas the second chorus removes the guitars and puts piano, synthesizer, and additional percussion in the foreground. The outro contracts to bass, drums, piano, and electric guitar, with a more focused palette than the choruses. Rather than simply becoming thicker throughout, the arrangement rotates the emphasis among strings, two guitars, keyboards, and percussion over a stable bass-and-drum foundation.

questions.question_type: 同根大小属和弦对比
questions.question: In the second chorus, major and minor triads appear in succession on the same root. What is the function and actual destination of each, and which one returns more directly to the tonic?
questions.reference_answer: The home key is D minor. The opening A major triad is V and contains the leading tone C#, but it actually moves first to Gm7 (iv7) rather than resolving immediately to Dm. Later, Am is v in natural minor and actually proceeds to Dm (i). questions.question_type: 全曲织体发展轨迹
questions.question: How does the instrumentation gradually expand and then contract from the opening through the two long main sections to the ending? Compare the core timbres, rhythmic thickness, and intermediate change of color at each stage.
questions.reference_answer: The opening is the thinnest, with harp, guitar, and a sustained synthesizer pad creating space before a full rhythm section has formed. The first long section adds drums, bass, acoustic and electric guitars, and synthesizer, expanding into the full ensemble. The short middle section removes the broad synth pad and uses electric guitar, acoustic guitar, drums, bass, and additional percussion for a more direct rock groove. The second long section restores the synth pad while retaining drums, bass, and both guitars as its foundation. The ending contracts again to bass, drums, and electric guitar, leaving a drier, more direct close. The overall path is “spacious opening—full-ensemble expansion—guitar/percussion recoloring—renewed expansion—contraction to three core parts.”

questions.question_type: 段内和声节奏变化
questions.question: Listen to the second long main section. Does the rate of harmonic change remain constant? Summarize the shifts in speed across its opening, middle, and ending, and explain how they affect the sense of forward motion.
questions.reference_answer: The rate is not constant. In the first roughly eight measures, the harmony changes mainly every one or two measures, including one C-to-D change within a single measure, making the direction most active. In the middle, blocks such as Em, C, and D are generally stretched to about two measures, slowing the rate and broadening the sound. Near the ending, paired D6 and Cmaj7 events and a final D reorganize the harmony; the pace tightens slightly but still retains broad areas of prolongation. The resulting motion has three stages: relatively fast and irregular, broad two-measure blocks, then renewed concentration at the end.

questions.question_type: 段落和声框架提取
questions.question: Listen to the first lead-instrument section and reduce it to its main harmonic framework. How does the first half linger between two stable colors, and which three-chord progression in the latter half clearly returns to the center? Give the actual chords, Roman numerals, and functions.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is E minor. The section begins on Cmaj7 (VImaj7), moves to Em/Em7 (i/i7), and briefly returns to Cmaj7; the first half therefore lingers in broad blocks between the bright color of VImaj7 and the tonic function of i/i7. D major (VII) then moves into Em (i), and the clearest framework in the latter half is C→D→Em, or VI→VII→i. C/VI carries subdominant-direction or predominant color, and D/VII, the natural minor's lowered seventh degree, actually proceeds to Em/i, restoring tonic function. The section does not use B7 (V7) for a traditional authentic cadence.

questions.question_type: 电子配器的段落对比
questions.question: How does this short piece use electronic timbres, guitar, and cymbals to create layers across four stages? Summarize the changes in instrumentation at the opening, the long main section, the contrasting middle passage, and the ending.
questions.reference_answer: The opening forms a compact three-layer electronic texture from synth lead, synth bass, and drums. The long main section adds more synthesizer, synth pad, and percussion, producing the most sustained and full-bodied layering. The contrasting middle passage foregrounds electric guitar, cymbals, and bass while retaining drums, synth lead, and synth bass, creating a sharper timbre and a brief burst of energy. The ending removes electric guitar and cymbals, returning to synthesizer, synth bass, bass, and drums as the sound contracts again. Rather than relying on many new chords to articulate the form, the piece thickens its electronic layers, recolors them with guitar and cymbals, and then returns to its electronic core.

questions.question_type: 半音下属和弦的解决分析
questions.question: Listen to the final section. Analyze the actual resolution of its opening major chord with a minor seventh, then give the recurring harmonic framework that follows. Using the actual successor chords, state the home key, chords, Roman numerals, and functions.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is E minor. The section opens with A7=IV7. Its chromatic C# can be understood as the bright color of a subdominant borrowed from E Dorian or melodic minor. Within the same measure, it resolves directly to Em=i, so the actual progression is a blues- or rock-colored IV7→i return. Although the spelling of A7 may suggest V7/V, it does not resolve to D here and therefore should not be classified as a completed secondary-dominant resolution. The subsequent framework is Em→Cmaj7→D→Em, or i→VImaj7→VII→i, followed once more by Cmaj7→D and then silence. Cmaj7 provides predominant color, D/VII supplies forward motion, and its actual target is the tonic Em chord.

questions.question_type: 单段曲式的织体与动态分区
questions.question: The piece has only one formal section, but its internal density is not uniform. Based solely on the sound, how would you divide its internal layers? Compare the dynamics, foreground attack density, and rate of timbral change in each stage, and identify the band foundation that remains constant throughout.
questions.reference_answer: It can be heard as four internal layers. From the opening through the first return of the material, drums and bass maintain a steady pulse while electric guitar, acoustic guitar, synthesizer, and cymbals create a relatively continuous foreground. The overall level is stable and harmonic colors change fairly often. A clear contraction follows: the overall level and high-frequency attacks decrease, the foreground leaves more space, and the harmony remains unchanged for a long time, making the material feel compressed into a suspended platform. In the latter half, attacks from the rhythm section, guitars, and cymbals grow denser again, the energy rises, and a regular short loop drives the music onward. The final seconds thin out and fade once more. The ensemble never changes wholesale: drums, bass, two guitars, synthesizer, and cymbals remain the shared foundation. The changing activity density, dynamic envelope, and rate of timbral change within that same ensemble create the internal divisions.

questions.question_type: 全曲调性变化判断
questions.question: The final section suddenly becomes brighter and higher. Does it merely emphasize a chromatic chord, or is there a genuine modulation? Give the original key, target key, pivotal progression, and evidence that the new key persists.
questions.reference_answer: This is a genuine modulation from D♭ major to E♭ major, moving the tonic up by a major second rather than merely introducing a brief chromatic chord. Before the modulation, Ebm→Db→Db closes the old key, with Db functioning as its tonic I. The music then enters directly on Eb; from the new perspective, the old tonic Db can be heard as a ♭VII color in the new key moving upward to Eb/I. After the modulation, the actual progression is Eb→Bb/D→Cm→Gm→Ab→Eb6/Cm7→Fm→Bb7sus4→Eb, corresponding to I→V6→vi→iii→IV→I(add6)/vi7→ii→V7sus4→I. E♭-major harmony then remains in force through the end, which repeatedly rests on Eb. Because the target key persists to the end of the piece, this is a structural modulation.

questions.reference_answer: It is a rewritten and reharmonized version that preserves the rhythmic framework, not an exact intervallic transposition. The first block is supported by Bm/Bm7 (i/i7) and begins with B as the bass anchor; the second is supported by G/Gmaj7 (VI/VImaj7) and changes the anchor to G. Both use many continuous eighth notes, similar short figures, and shared pitches such as C#, D, and A, making their common origin audible. However, the later intervals and points of arrival in the second block are rearranged around the G chord rather than maintaining one transposition interval for every pitch. The second block's actual successor returns to Bm/i.

questions.question_type: 相同和弦开头的不同去向
questions.question: Listen to the latter half of the long lead-instrument section. A four-chord chain appears twice in immediate succession, but a different chord follows each occurrence. Give the chain and its Roman numerals, and compare how the first and second occurrences handle the expected return.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is B minor. The repeated chain is G→Em→F#m→A, or VI→iv→v→VII; F#m is the minor dominant v, and A is VII in natural minor. After the first occurrence, the actual successor of A/VII is Bm/i, creating the modal return VI→iv→v→VII→i. The second likewise reaches A/VII, but its actual successor is G/VI rather than Bm, yielding the sectional continuation VI→iv→v→VII→VI and postponing tonic resolution. Neither occurrence uses F#7/V7, so although the first lands on the tonic, it is not a traditional leading-tone-driven authentic cadence. The changed target in the second creates a sense of continued development.

questions.question_type: 跨段前景音色与织体发展
questions.question: From the opening through the long main section to the ending, how does this instrumental piece create formal layers by handing off foreground timbres and pad roles? For each section, identify which timbres are added, removed, or substituted, and which rhythmic and low-frequency parts continue throughout.
questions.reference_answer: The opening is a compact four-layer electronic texture: synth lead carries the foreground, synth bass and ordinary bass combine in the low end, and drums maintain the pulse. Electric guitar, strings, and a broad synth pad are not yet present. In the long main section, synth lead and synth bass leave the listed instrumentation, electric guitar assumes the more prominent foreground role, and synthesizer plus synth pad broaden the middle- and high-frequency space; drums and bass continue as the stable foundation. The ending retains drums, bass, electric guitar, synthesizer, and pad, then adds strings, giving the electronic-rock texture a broader, more tensile orchestral color. The three sections are thus distinguished not by a change of key but by the foreground handoff “synth lead and doubled low end—guitar and pad substitution—strings joining the hybrid texture,” while drums and bass remain throughout.

questions.question_type: 主和弦延长与释放
questions.question: Listen to the main section. Why does its first half sound almost harmonically static, and why does the latter half suddenly regain direction? Identify the sustained chord and the actual progression that follows.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is F minor. The section initially carries over Eb=VII, after which Fm=i is prolonged from bar 17 through bar 36 without a fundamental chord change. The first half therefore resembles a tonic pedal, with tension generated primarily through timbre and rhythm. From bar 37, the progression Db=VI, Eb=VII, Fm=i appears: VI→VII→i. Db actually proceeds to Eb, which then returns to Fm, restoring harmonic motion. Near the end, the section moves once more toward Db→Eb, preserving forward momentum into the next section.

questions.question_type: 末段终止状态与和声去向判断
questions.question: Listen to the final section. Does it ultimately create clear closure or preserve a sense of continuation? Give the complete harmonic framework and Roman numerals, including every actual destination, and support your judgment using the final labeled chord and the sound that follows.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is F minor. The section begins on Eb=VII, which actually proceeds to Fm=i. After its prolongation, Fm moves to Db=VI and then to Eb=VII, followed by a three-measure tail with no new chord label. The reduced framework is VII→i→VI→VII→silence. The earlier Eb has a clear successor, Fm, and therefore completes one modal return. The final Eb, however, is followed by neither another Fm nor an authentic C7/V7→Fm resolution. The piece therefore does not close clearly on the tonic; it stops after the propulsive lowered-seventh chord and lets the sound dissipate, producing an open ending.

questions.reference_answer: The tonic is D♭, and the overall key is D♭ major. Db/Dbmaj7 and their inversions repeatedly serve as I. Ebm7→Ab→Db forms ii7→V→I, while F or F/A briefly tonicizes B♭m as vi; none of these displaces the D♭-major center. The final section also returns to Db.

questions.question_type: 跨段主题材料关系比较
questions.question: Compare the principal melodic material in the first short section, the long main section, and the final short section. Which pitch motions make the three recognizable as related, and how do their register, attack density, and phrase length change? Use actual pitches to determine whether the latter two are exact repetitions or transformations of different degrees.
questions.reference_answer: At the end of the first short section, two measures present the core contour: repeated B♭4s rise through C5 to D♭5 and then fall to A♭4. The long main section retains the identifying pattern of “repeated note—upward reach—return,” but adds longer continuous phrases and more short notes, expanding the range to approximately B♭3–G♭5. It is therefore an expanded variation, not an exact repetition. The final short section compresses the material into several stepwise turns: G♭4–F4–G♭4–A♭4, followed by A♭4–C5–D♭5, and then C5 into a prolonged D♭5. It preserves the directions of upward reach and return while shortening the phrases, making it a compressed transformation.

questions.question_type: 短主题的旋律轮廓与节奏
questions.question: Listen to the two-measure melody at the end of the first short section. How does it rise from a repeated pitch to its high point, fall back, and then make a second upward reach? Where do its longer notes chiefly occur?
questions.reference_answer: The melody begins with B♭4 held for a dotted-quarter-note duration, accelerates through two shorter repeated B♭4s, and rises in succession to C5 and the high point D♭5. It then falls to A♭4 and ties across into the next measure. From this sustained A♭4, the second measure leaps again to D♭5, moves through C5 back to D♭5, lingers on D♭5 for a longer dotted quarter note, and closes with a quarter-note A♭4. The longer notes cluster on the opening B♭4, the second D♭5, and the final A♭4, while the short-note ascents shape D♭5 as the phrase's two peaks.

questions.question_type: 功能性开头与低音下行
questions.question: Listen to the first short section. How does its first half establish the home key, and how do inversions and stepwise relations in the second half keep the harmony flowing downward? Give the actual chords and Roman numerals.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is D♭ major. The first half is Ebm7→Ab→Db, or ii7→V→I; Ab actually proceeds to Db, first giving clear confirmation of the home key. The second half is Ab/C→B♭m→Ab→Gb→Db/F, corresponding to V6→vi→V→IV→I6. Ab/C places C in the bass and Db/F places F in the bass; between them, the line passes through B♭, A♭, and G♭, creating a relatively continuous descending bass and harmonic regression. It ends on I6, the tonic in first inversion, rather than root-position I, simultaneously returning to tonic function and preserving a sense of ongoing flow.

questions.question_type: 次属和弦与借用下属和弦
questions.question: Listen to the long main section. Identify the two types of secondary dominant that complete their resolutions, along with one chord borrowed from the parallel minor. For each, give the actual chord, Roman numeral or inversion, target chord, and function.
questions.reference_answer: The home key is D♭ major. The first secondary dominant is Eb7=V7/V, whose actual successor is Ab=V, completing a tonicization of the dominant. The second type comprises F/A and F: F/A is V6/vi and F is V/vi, and both actually proceed to B♭m=vi, briefly tonicizing the submediant minor chord; A, the third of the F major triad, is placed in the bass of F/A. The borrowed chord is G♭m=iv, from the parallel key D♭ minor. Its actual successor is Ab=V; through chromatic voice leading such as B♭♭, heard enharmonically as A natural, it adds a darker color and serves a borrowed subdominant or predominant function. After completing their local motions, all three types return to the D♭-major framework and establish no lasting new key.
